'''Mathilde B. "Mimi" Lee''' (May 1, 1920&nbsp;– August 9, 2011) was an American [[chemist]], [[sportsperson|athlete]] and [[philanthropist]] who served as the [[List of First Spouses of Maryland|First Lady]] of [[Maryland]] from 1977 to 1979 when her husband, then Lt. Governor [[Blair Lee III]], became acting governor following the departure of [[Governor of Maryland|Governor]] [[Marvin Mandel]].<ref name=bsun>{{cite news|first=Frederick N. |last=Rasmussen |title=Mathilde B. "Mimi" Lee, former acting first lady of Maryland, dies at 91 |url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2011/08/13/mathilde-b-mimi-lee-former-acting-first-lady-of-maryland-dies-at-91/ |work=[[Baltimore Sun]] |date=2011-08-13 |access-date=2011-09-08 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121002063009/http://articles.baltimoresun.com/2011-08-13/news/bs-md-ob-mathilde-lee-20110812_1_first-lady-canoe-direct-descendant |archive-date=2012-10-02 }}</ref><ref name=wp>{{cite news|first=Adam|last=Bernstein |title=Mimi Lee, wife of former Maryland governor Blair Lee III, dies at 91 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/obituaries/mimi-lee-wife-of-former-maryland-governor-blair-lee-iii-dies-at-91/2011/08/11/gIQAuzlU9I_story.html |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=2011-08-11|access-date=2011-09-10}}</ref><ref name=cs>{{cite news |title='Mimi' Lee, former Maryland first lady, remembered as woman of faith and action |url=http://www.catholicstandard.com/main.asp?SectionID=2&SubSectionID=27&ArticleID=4726&TM=17958.9 |work=[[Catholic Standard]] |date=2011-08-16 |access-date=2011-09-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402132135/http://www.catholicstandard.com/main.asp?SectionID=2&SubSectionID=27&ArticleID=4726&TM=17958.9 |archive-date=2012-04-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Biography==

===Early life===
Lee was born '''Mathilde Boal''' on May 1, 1920, in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name=wp/> She was named for her paternal grandmother, a distant relative of [[Christopher Columbus]].<ref name=bsun/> Her mother, Jeanne de Menthon, a native of [[France]], was a [[Lineal descendant|descendant]] of the 11th century French [[saint]], [[Bernard of Menthon]].<ref name=bsun/> Lee's father, [[Pierre de Lagarde Boal]], was an American diplomat who served as the United States' ambassador to [[Nicaragua]] and [[Bolivia]] during the 1940s.<ref name=wp/> Boal, who was fluent in [[English language|English]], [[French language|French]] and [[Spanish language|Spanish]], lived in ten countries by the time she completed college.<ref name=bsun/>

Boal graduated from [[Elmwood School (Ottawa)|Elmwood School]], an exclusive all-girls school in [[Ottawa|Ottawa, Ontario]], Canada, where her father was stationed for a diplomatic post.<ref name=bsun/> She obtained a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[chemistry]] in 1943, graduating [[cum laude]] from [[Bryn Mawr College]] in [[Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania]].<ref name=wp/>

Boal took a job as a [[chemist]] with the [[Rockefeller Foundation]] in [[Colombia]] after graduating from Bryn Mawr College.<ref name=wp/> She soon became engaged to [[Blair Lee III|Francis Preston Blair Lee III]], a [[naval officer]] during [[World War II]], whom she married in 1944.<ref name=bsun/> The two families, the Lees and the Boals, had previously been close friends even before the marriage.<ref name=bsun/> The couple had eight children.<ref name=cs/>

===First Lady of Maryland===
Blair Lee III was sworn in as [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland]] in 1971 and became acting [[Governor of Maryland|Governor]] in 1977 when Governor [[Marvin Mandel]] was charged with [[racketeering]] and stepped down on an interim basis. As Maryland's First Lady, Lee took on an unusually independent approach from her predecessors.<ref name=wp/> Lee did not move to the [[Government House (Maryland)|Government House]] in [[Annapolis]] instead choosing to live with her children full-time at their home and [[farm]] in [[Silver Spring, Maryland]].<ref name=wp/> When speaking to the ''[[Baltimore Sun]]'' upon taking office in 1978, Governor Lee said of his wife, "Where I go, she goes. At least that's what I keep telling myself anyway. She would rather be [[canoeing]] on the [[Potomac River|Potomac]], [[backpacking (wilderness)|backpacking]] along the [[Appalachian Trail]] or teaching children to swim than preparing for a formal party."<ref name=bsun/> One of Lee's predecessors, former First Lady [[Barbara Mandel]], publicly offered to act as a "sort of senior adviser" to Lee explaining the need of First Ladies to engage in ceremonies, such as [[ribbon cutting]]s and garden tours.<ref name=yv>{{cite news|title=Mrs. Mandel is Mentor To Her Successor |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=JxJJAAAAIBAJ&pg=2648,1962407&dq=mimi+lee+maryland&hl=en |work=[[Youngstown Vindicator]] |date=1977-10-20|access-date=2011-09-17}}</ref>

Lee privately and publicly disliked much of the ceremonial roles of a traditional First Lady, like the ribbon cuttings, and the practice of [[politics]], which she called "frivolous."<ref name=bsun/><ref name=wp/> Political [[columnist]] [[Frank DeFilippo]], who served as [[press secretary]] for Governor Mandel, said of Lee, "I normally eschew the overused word 'unique,' but Mimi truly was. I've covered first ladies going back to [[Avalynne Tawes]], and Mimi was the only one of the bunch who truly loathed life in the [[mansion]], which, when forced to be there, she roamed in [[Sunny's Surplus]] fatigues with cargo pockets."<ref name=bsun/> Lee compared the formal role of First Lady, which she called "pomp," to social functions held at [[U.S. embassies]] when she was a girl.<ref name=wp/> In a 1977 article, the ''[[Washington Post]]'' took note of the unusual outlook of the new First Lady, "She disdains [[luncheon]]s and [[fashion shows]] except for her favorite causes — the [[Red Cross]], [[water safety]] and [[Holy Cross Hospital (Silver Spring)|Holy Cross Hospital]] among others. And while some other women from ordinary backgrounds would revel in the new status, Mimi Lee admits that sometimes it's inconvenient."<ref name=bsun/> The ''Washington Post'' also noted that she "answers her own phone, vacuums her house, cooks for her guests."<ref name=bsun/> In 1977, she told the ''Washington Post'' she wanted to "throw up" whenever her family was described as an "[[aristocracy]]."<ref name=bsun/>

While Lee limited her time in the state capitol, she partook in her state duties when necessary.<ref name=wp/> Even in [[Annapolis]], Lee preferred sneakers, jeans and work skirts to more formal attire.<ref name=bsun/><ref name=wp/> She once expressed irritation at the cancellation of a [[white water rafting]] trip on the [[Shenandoah River]], but later told the ''Washington Post'' in the late 1970s that she had a "lovely" time hosting [[Anne, Princess Royal|The Princess Anne]].<ref name=wp/> Lee focused much of her official time as First Lady on volunteer functions, such as the [[March of Dimes]] or the Red Cross.<ref name=wp/> An accomplished [[sportsperson|athlete]], Lee taught swimming classes for the handicapped while in office.<ref name=wp/> She held an annual "Beer Bash" for Maryland Democrats at her farm in Silver Spring, often cooking for the guests.<ref name=bsun/>

Governor Blair Lee ran for a full term as governor in 1978, but was defeated in the Democratic gubernatorial primary by [[Harry Hughes]].<ref name=wp/><ref name=cs/> The Lees left office in January 1979, shortly before the end of his term, when Governor Mendel reclaimed his office for the two remaining days.<ref name=wp/>

===Later life===
Her husband, Blair Lee, died in 1985. Lee devoted much of the rest of her life to athletic and [[philanthropic]] pursuits.<ref name=cs/> Lee was an avid [[outdoor enthusiast]] throughout her life, pursuing [[skiing]], [[canoeing]], and [[camping]].<ref name=wp/> She became a practitioner of [[yoga]] during her tenure as First Lady and continued her athletic interests during her later life, becoming a competitive Senior athlete in swimming.<ref name=wp/>

An accomplished [[Senior Olympics|Senior Olympian]], Lee broke numerous national and Maryland [[Swimming (sport)|swimming]] records while competing in the [[Senior Olympics]] during the 1990s.<ref name=bsun/><ref name=wp/><ref name=gazette>{{cite news|first=Kristi|last=Tousignant|title=Mimi Lee, wife of former governor, dies|url=http://www.gazette.net/article/20110810/NEWS/708109353/wife-of-former-gov-blair-lee-iii-dies&template=gazette|work=[[The Gazette (Maryland)]]|date=2011-08-10|access-date=2011-09-17|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120829144111/http://www.gazette.net/article/20110810/NEWS/708109353/wife-of-former-gov-blair-lee-iii-dies%26template%3Dgazette|archive-date=2012-08-29}}</ref><ref name=mso>{{cite news|title=All-Time Aquatics Records – Maryland Senior Olympics |url=http://www.mdseniorolympics.org/pdf/swimming_records2010.pdf |work=Maryland Senior Olympics |date=2011-08-10|access-date=2011-09-17}}</ref> Lee also competed in the [[Masters athletics|U.S. Masters Swimming Nationals]], winning eight swimming competitions throughout the United States, and placed second in twenty other races.<ref name=bsun/> She hiked the [[Pyrenees]] between [[France]] and [[Spain]] with two of her seventeen-year-old grandchildren when she was seventy years old.<ref name=bsun/>

Outside of [[swimming]], Lee learned [[German language|German]] during her 80s.<ref name=bsun/>

Mimi Lee died of [[congestive heart failure]] at [[Laurel Regional Hospital]] in [[Laurel, Maryland]], on August 9, 2011, at the age of 91.<ref name=wp/><ref name=cs/> She was survived by seven of her eight children&nbsp;– Blair Lee IV, Joseph W. Lee, Christopher G. Lee, Erica B. Lee, Philip L. Lee, John F. Lee and Jenny Sataloff; her sister, Mary Elizabeth d'Harcourt; nineteen grandchildren and four great-grandchildren.<ref name=wp/> Another son, Pierre B. Lee, died in 1973. Lee's [[funeral Mass]] was held at her parish, St. John the Baptist Catholic Church, in Silver Spring.<ref name=cs/>
